text_fidelity_a:
LensPen NLP-1C Lens Cleaner (Black with Gold Rings) This lens pen is just what I need in a compact, easy-to-carry product. I am a photographer who has to carry a lot of gear outside. Having something compact and light is essential.

One side is a brush to get rid of fine and large particles of material from the lens. The other side is to remove oils (e.g. fingerprints) and is made of a fine material that has a carbon dust cleaning solution embedded in it.

The first three to five uses can be a bit frustrating as this carbon dust is quite heavy and will actually leave a slight residue on the lens. In this case I just used the brush first, the carbon cleaner second, and then finished up with the brush again to remove any extra carbon. I had no artifacts in my photos at all. After the initial break-in period this lens pen performs flawlessly.

The pen is close to 4 inches long (without the brush extended) and about 3/4 inches wide. Its actually very compact and light. It has a tab on the cap to be able to secure it while its in a pocket, just like a regular pen. The brush is about an inch long and is used by extending it out of the end of the pen. It adds about an inch of length when extended. The carbon cleaner is covered by a cap which is screwed off in order to expose the cleaning surface. I wish there was a spot to put this cap while using the carbon cleaning side. Its the only long term con to this pen.

Pros:
*Light
*Compact
*Cleans lenses well
*Easy to carry in pocket
*Cheap

Cons:
*Carbon dust residue for first 3-5 uses.(-1/4 star)
*Cap has no place to be put on the pen while using it. (-1/4 star)

Overall 4.5/5 (>=.5 rounds up, <.5 rounds down) => 5 star rating

If you have any further questions regarding the product in my review please leave a comment below and I will get back to you as soon as possible.
text_fidelity_b: LensPen NLP-1C Lens Cleaner (Black with Gold Rings)

Logitech Wireless Speaker Adapter for Bluetooth Audio Devices There really isn't a lot to say about this adapter, which is a good thing--it just does what it says it does and does so seamlessly and easily.

"installation" couldn't be easier
1) plug it in to the wall
2) cable it to your stereo with the attached cable/wire
3) pair it with your bluetooth device
4) play your music

My review is limited to connecting via my Apple devices: a Touch and a laptop. Both worked without any issues whatsoever. I noticed that some reviewers have said they need to repair each time; I haven't experienced that problem. I bring my Touch back into the house, turn on the stereo, hit play on the Touch, and out it comes.

I am not an audiophile by any stretch of the imagination so keep that in mind, but personally I don't notice any drop off in quality when it plays through. Nor does it ever drop the signal.

It's small, discrete, easy to hide or blend in with your stereo. It sits there unobtrusively and lets me play my music collection or Pandora without any hassle of set-up or maintenance. It just works. Highly recommended!

text_fidelity_a:
Bose SoundTouch 10 wireless speaker, works with Alexa - Black Before writing this review I glanced over some reviews of earlier models, and whatever issues previous editions of the Bose SoundTouch speakers may have had seem to have been worked out with this SoundTouch 10.

Setup was simple with the SoundTouch app (available for iOS, Android, and Kindle Fire devices). We had the speaker set up and operating in less than 5 minutes using an iPad. You'll need your home network security code to connect to WiFi and that's about it.

It comes with a remote, but most of the controlling is done from your device (tablet or phone). The remote is handy for adjusting the volume when you're using your device for other things.

The speaker is about the size of a cereal box. The sound that comes out is impressive for its size. I think there's a wee bit of case resonance in the mid range, but that's just me -- everyone else thinks it sounds terrific. It doesn't rival a huge stereo system but it's really, really good.

Now excuse me while I get on my soapbox about monaural. This is a single speaker system, not stereo, and that, to me, is a good thing. I'm a fan of monaural. It solves a lot of issues about speaker placement (trying to make sure they're equally distant), and you hear the full mix as the producers and artists intended. You can move anywhere around the room and not have half the mix disappear. And if you like oldies, particularly from the 1960s, this fixes the problems caused by common pan/mix practices from that era (for example, drums and bass panned hard left, guitars and backup singers panned hard right, lead vocals in the middle). If you listen to mixes like that in headphones, you pretty much have to mix the music down in your imagination since bass/drums are exclusively in one ear and keyboards in the other. Some devices don't support mono audio output (I'm looking at you, Windows phone), and as far as I know no one makes a dual-ear mono headset for phones either. So a mono speaker solves the issue. Okay, that's it for the soapbox. Back to the review.

The only tone control available in the Bose app is bass volume. But since the sound is well engineered, it's adequate. And bass is very audible. Not subwoofer level audible, but it's very present.

The SoundTouch app itself is impressive. It really does make setup a breeze. And the listening options are VAST. Hundreds of radio stations from around the world on WiFi, streaming music services, Pandora, Spotify, and so forth. I used to do a little shortwave listening, and if you're a DXer, this exceeds the capability of SW by far, and every station is digitally clear. And you can connect directly to play music straight from your device.

Just to be clear, the speaker itself needs a wall outlet to power it. It's not battery powered. But everything else is wireless. More speakers can be added, but it's so easily unplugged and moved around that one speaker can easily be sufficient.

Nice product from Bose.
text_fidelity_b: Bose SoundTouch 10 wireless speaker, works with Alexa - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Surge Protector Power Strip with USB, Silicone Extension Cord with 10 Outlets 3 USB Charging Ports and 1 USB-C Charging Port, 1875W/15A Overload Surge Protection, Gift for Mother's Day PROS

1. It has 10 sockets/outlets.
2. Two of the sockets are offset from the other six. This allows them to be used for wide plugs, which is an important feature, because wide plugs are a frequent occurrence on appliances.
3. The color is an attractive but neutral black which makes the strip fade into the background more than the strips I own which are white or beige.
4. In addition to being a power strip, it also provides surge protection.
5. There are four USB ports that can be used for charging devices. One of them is a USB-C port and the other 3 are standard USB ports. The manufacturer claims in the manual that the three standard USB ports are “smart” USB ports.

CONS

1. I am not entirely comfortable trusting the “smart” USB ports on this device for charging. I feel more comfortable using a regular USB charging adapter and plugging it into a socket on the surge protector side of this device.

2. Regarding the smart USB ports, there are not adequate instructions either in the manual or on the manufacturer’s website that clearly explain the implications of this feature and how to utilize it. I cannot find information on the top mA it supports in charging.

GENERAL INFORMATION ON USB CHARGING

In order to test this device for my Vine review, I spent over two hours (!!!) trying to find comprehensible information on what the term “smart” means in the context of a USB port on a power strip like this one. Unfortunately, I was left with more questions than answers, for which hassle I’m dropping a star off this review. I’ve included some of what I learned below, for what it might be worth to any fellow Amazon customer who might be thinking of purchasing this product.

A smart USB charger port supposedly can, in and of itself, figure out what the optimal charging speed of a specific device is when it is plugged into that port, in order to neither overload it with too much current or under-deliver to it the optimal current. The question on everyone’s mind these days (it certainly has been on mine), is whether it is possible to destroy the battery in a particular device by slamming too much current into it. Apparently, the answer to this all-important question is: No. If, for example, you take a phone which comes with a 900mA wall charger, and you plug it into a 2,100mA charger that comes with a different device you own, it will not damage the phone. It will only speed up the length of time it takes for the phone’s battery to charge. However, if you have a USB device older than 2007, it may not charge on any USB ports newer than the (now ancient), 500mA USB 1.0 and 2.0 PC ports. Which means such older devices may not charge even on the “smart” USB ports on this device.

USB charging current is measured in mA (milliampere, 1/1000 of an ampere, the basic unit for measuring electrical current). There are three kinds of USB ports which are defined by their current specs: a standard downstream port, a charging downstream port, and a dedicated charging port. The first two are found on a desktop computer. The third kind is a “dumb” wall charger.

USB 1.0 and 2.0 standard downstream ports on a computer can deliver up to 500mA (0.5A).

USB 3.0 standard downstream ports on a computer can deliver up to 900mA (0.9A).

USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 ports can deliver between 1,500mA (1.5A) and 3,000mA (3A).

Charging downstream USB ports on a computer can deliver up to 1,500mA (1.5A).

Dedicated USB charging ports on a computer can deliver up to 3,000mA (3A).
text_fidelity_b: Surge Protector Power Strip with USB, Silicone Extension Cord with 10 Outlets 3 USB Charging Ports and 1 USB-C Charging Port, 1875W/15A Overload Surge Protection, Gift for Mother's Day

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Fire HD 8 tablet, 8” HD Display, 32 GB, 30% faster processor, designed for portable entertainment, (2022 release), Rose TL;DR

The Kindle Fire HD 8 is a serviceable tablet if you don’t intend to use it for much outside of consuming media, primarily from Amazon’s in-house apps. If you’re interested, I recommend that you wait until they’re on sale before making the purchase.

Full Review:

I bought my Kindle Fire HD 8 primarily for listening to music. I use Amazon Music (Unlimited subscriber) and it has a headphone jack. Not wanting to deal with the ads from the lockscreen, I paid to have them removed. Over the past few weeks, I’ve been playing around with the device to see what it’s capable of when it comes to media consumption. Here’s what I’ve come up with! I did manage to sideload Google Play and several apps. I’ll reflect on those experiences, though any issues I had from this will not count against the device, as Google Play and the apps from it are not officially supported.

Interface and Build Quality
You are pretty much stuck with their stock interface. You can’t remove ANY of the Amazon apps from the homescreen. However, you can hide them away in a folder. This cleaned things up, nicely. Toward the top of the screen, you have a static bar that shows your last 2 apps, as well as some recommended apps. They do manage to sneak a sponsored app in there from time to time. Seeing that I paid to get rid of ads, this annoyed me (though it really doesn’t impact my use.) I actually like typing on this more than I do my Samsung Galaxy Tab S6 Lite or my Samsung S22 phone, which surprised me. One would think they’d make sure their own apps are working on their own devices at least as well as the apps work on their competitors devices.

The tablet itself feels kinda cheap, but not as cheap as I expected. The screen’s glass isn’t as smooth as my Samsung devices, but it’s quite functional. You can tell there’s not much power under the hood, as apps take a few seconds to load, and there’s sometimes interface lag when interacting with them. The onboard speakers suck, but I don’t use them. Headphones are the way to go… and since it has a headphone jack, I’m all set. The display is plenty for what I use it for.

Support
I’ve reached out to Amazon a few times to ask questions, or to get help. They’ve been incredibly responsive. The reps have always been courteous and informative. High marks here!

Audio and Video Quality
Music sounds great through my Audio Technica ATH-M50x headphones, especially HD and Ultra HD from Amazon Music. Strangely, the app does not have an EQ option (I can adjust the EQ on my Windows PC and on my other Android devices.) It supports my Fosi Audio DS1 with no problems. This improves the sound a bit (mostly making things a bit louder.) It did not power up my Fosi Audio K5 Pro, however. Unfortunately, the Kindle Fire HD 8 did not support my Bluetooth Audio Technica ATH-SR50BT’s, which was a disappointment. On the flipside, I was able to sideload 4Stream and the Andover Songbird app to get it to stream HD audio to my Denon D-M41, which was a pleasant surprise.

I took some time to watch some streaming video via Prime Video, Netflix and YouTube (sideloaded via Google Play.) Even though it’s not a true “HD” display, the screen is small enough to make it not matter so much. Lord of the Rings - Fellowship of the Rings probably benefited from this, as the movie didn’t age well in our HD world. The audio on it was also quite engaging through my headphones. Ash vs the Evil Dead on Netflix also streamed flawlessly, and looked great on the screen. YouTube videos play just fine as well, even though the app was sideloaded.

As an eReader
The Kindle Fire HD 8 works great as an eReader, as one would expect. Since I don’t plan to read much from it, I didn’t explore it much. Books loaded just fine, and you can interact with them as you’d expect (the Kindle is pretty robust for this, for those who’re interested.)

Non-media Consumption
I tried getting Discord to work on the Fire HD 8. While I was able to install it, the experience was pretty terrible. Browsing the internet with the Silk browser leaves some to be desired, and the mail/calendar apps are not something I’m interested in using. Again, I’m using this primarily for music, so I’m fine with this. However, if I needed to use it for anything productive, I’d be quite frustrated.

Google Play
Instructions on how to get Google Play installed are readily available online, and it’s easily doable within an hour’s time. I was able to install an EQ for my music, which works okay (I did have the app crash once.) The Gmail app loaded fairly well, as did Google Chrome. However, I can’t sync Chrome, as my email account was already used to activate the Kindle. There haven’t been any issues with YouTube. Dragon Quest 1 and 2 installed flawlessly and seem to work fine. However, Baldur’s Gate 1 & 2, along with other Beamdog games did not install at all (these aren’t officially supported, but folks claim it works. Not for me!) Again, none of these experiences with Google Play will count for or against my overall rating for this device. I’m simply stating them in case anyone else is interested in tinkering.

Ultimately, the Kindle Fire HD 8 is okay for the money (when on sale.) It works for my purposes, but I can tell it’d leave a lot to be desired if I wanted to use it for anything more. The fact that they still advertise apps on the home screen, even after you pay to remove ads is annoying (enough to knock my rating down a star.) I do suspect that the Kindle Fire devices are probably loss-leaders, and any ads they can cram in help generate income.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Fire HD 8 tablet, 8” HD Display, 32 GB, 30% faster processor, designed for portable entertainment, (2022 release), Rose

First the things I like about this Camcorder:
This camcorder records in high definition (1020 at 30 fps), and two low resolution (720P at both 30 and 60 fps) select-able from the screen.
There is a option for setting the camera up for motion control triggered recording.
The system has a IR based night vision system to record in total blackout conditions.
The remote can be used to control most modes of the camcorder and start/stop recording.
This system comes with a external mic to help in recording the audio component of your filming, you have the option to use this mic or not depending on your circumstances.
You can use the camcorder as a photo camera with resolutions ranging from 5mp to 24mp along with settings for white balance, color, and shutter speeds.
You can turn off the beep sound for camera functions, something you may use if recording wildlife.
This Camcorder comes with a wide view lens, great when recording in a shallow area such as a room to get everyone and everything into one shot.
Extra battery, handy for extended use or areas where you cannot recharge the camera.

Things I would like to see improved:
The zoom is digital only, not an optical zoom. This limits the camcorder to recording only items in a shallow depth, not great for outdoor use unless you are up close to your subject.

All in all, a decent camcorder for use where you are close (physically) to your subject, or as long as you understand its limitations.

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra SPORT Bluetooth Stereo Headset - Black/Yellow (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I am disappointed with these headphones for only one reason: My ears are small, and because of that, these headphones will not snuggly "hang" over my ears like they should. (Children would have the same problem, I expect.) If the over-ear part of the headphones were a little more moldable, I might be able to make them work for me; the extra ear gels themselves are helpful in getting a good fit into the ear canal, but that doesn't keep them from falling off of me. This is why I'm knocking of a star but, again, the problem is not with the headset but with my own anatomy!

With that caveat aside, I love them! For a gardener who wants to listen to something outside while working, the FM radio works just fine and the yellow rubbery cord keeps them around your neck even if you do knock them off. The U.S. Military-grade protection features (against dust, moisture, and shock) make these headphones stand out from the pack.

The Bluetooth pairing and sustained connection with these is better than any other Bluetooth device I've ever used, although I tend not to use Bluetooth unless I'm up and about in the house doing chores. I also don't make or get a lot of phone calls, so we don't even have a cellphone account and depend on the occasional VoIP to get the job done. Meaning I haven't tested the headset features at all.

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Technology Speaker - for Portable use - USB This speaker set sounds great for its size. The sound is loud and clear, but also full in the way you would expect stereo sound to be. It is also small enough to travel fairly easily, although it is not the smallest on the market. This is capable of getting louder than you'll ever be able to use in a hotel room, but suitable for an apartment; there are plenty of options out there in the form of travel speakers.

The built in mic is obviously a significant factor, and it works great compared to my laptop mic. I do like the fact that it gets its power and signal over one cable, but sometimes I think I'm going to run out of USB ports since I use them regularly to charge my phones and other devices. And I was also expecting bluetooth after seeing the ads for the other models. But who cares about bluetooth when you still need power?-smaller speakers don't need an external power source.

This is a good product and I'm certain to use it, especially when travelling for long enough that I want to set up more of a "home" that includes music. It is sort of another take on what is already a niche product, however, and although I do think it's one of the better styles on the market, it's still not the end all of small speakers, nor does it make dramatic improvements over what is already available. It's great at packing full sound into something very portable, and it eliminates one cable if you use USB, but then you use up another USB port. I'd love to see it either fully wireless with included battery or also include a webcam to preclude the need for other accessories. Yes, I know these things would up the cost, but it would make a truly remarkable product.

I also like how the invisible button panel appears when powered on, but not how you can't completely turn it off without removing the power source. The speaker looks good and I like how all sides are covered in speaker screen material, but I worry I could easily stick my finger through a cone.

A quality product that is great if it closely fits your needs.
text_fidelity_b: Creative Technology Speaker - for Portable use - USB

text_fidelity_a: Blink Video Doorbell | Two-way audio, HD video, motion and chime app alerts, and Alexa enabled — wired or wire-free (White) I am very impressed by this doorbell camera. I had been using a WYZE doorbell camera but that one could never connect to the Internet. Every time I complained they said it was my Internet connection which it’s not. I hooked the Blink up and I have not had one hiccup. The sensitivity is amazing I leave it set about midway and pick up car is going down the street I’ll have to make it a little less sensitive. Picture is very clear audio is good you can have a conversation with someone and they understand you so all in all I find it to be a great device. Nice thing is I had a grandfathered account with Blink so I didn’t have to buy the new siync module I use the old sync module and again have no problems. One other thing I was pleasantly surprised about I put the batteries in the doorbell camera and hooked it to my existing wiring so I could hear the doorbell ring in the house well, now it says that it’s on external power and running fine. That makes me even happier than ever  to not think about replacing the batteries every so often just keep it hooked to my doorbell wires and I’m in good shape. maybe some of the reviews that were written negatively on this product were when it first came out? From what I’m finding it’s pretty well refined and for the price you certainly can’t go wrong. My biggest complaint is I can’t get Alexa to integrate with my Blink cameras. None of them. I’ve tried all the troubleshooting techniques deleting and adding and it’s still not doesn’t work right. That’s only a minor flaw. But, like I say, for the price we can’t go wrong.
text_fidelity_b: Blink Video Doorbell | Two-way audio, HD video, motion and chime app alerts, and Alexa enabled — wired or wire-free (White)

Fitbit One Wireless Activity Plus Sleep Tracker, Black Three things have changed my life! FITBIT, Walking Workouts and Walking 4 Fun.

FITBIT ONE - I have been faithfully wearing it. Using the calories in and out featured on the app. It has a safety leash and I wear it attached to my bra. I do a Jessica Smith DVD - 10K Walking Workout (see link on bottom of this review) and Leslie Sansone ("Walk at Home"). However, ONE is super accurate on my walks outside and around the office. My bottom line is 10K steps a day but I tend to walk 17K a day. I worked my way up to this since October 2015. I have a sedentary job so walking happens 3 to 4 times a day with a minimum of a mile on each walk. Yes, I have lost weight, @ 40 lbs. There is at least that much more that needs to be lost as well. Hair color is silver if that helps you define the situation.

I love the little activity record feature and use it often (hold down the button to start and hold it down to end when activity is over). This is great when competing with friends where a challenge is inevitable. Speaking of friends. YEAH! That is where the FITBITs excel. I have a few friends in my community now and I love keeping up with them. Motivation features are fantastic!

This little baby doesn't buzz, which also means that the battery life is HUGE!! I think it goes 7 to 8 days before I need to be charged up. I tend to let it go dead because it warns you it needs to be charged about 1 1/2 days before it really does. I've only charged mine 3x now. It takes about an hour to charge. I wait until the visible battery = FULL!

This sweet little tracker is awesome! I started test driving the flex before getting the ONE which I also enjoyed but not as much as this one. I will buy the HR when this ONE dies or I just feel like bringing home another one. The reason I like this one better than the flex is because I don't tend to be an arm swinger and for me this one seems to work better (walking while pushing a cart). The best thing about the arm band models is that you affix it and forget it (until charging time) for which you should get a phone alert.

I don't bother with the sleep feature because I have an app (Sleep Cycle Alarm) on the phone that I use for which I love the beautiful melodious wake up sound. However the ONE comes with a little band for you to slide the ONE into obtain the reading for sleep.

Griffin Survivor Extreme-Duty Military Case for the iPad 4/3/2, Pink/Black (GB35379) With 3 little tech savvy kids in the house, ages 2-6, the electronics are a big draw. They hold a lot of appeal for the kids, but it's almost a constant stream of "oops!" as things are dropped when the kids move around or in a scuffle behind mom and dad's back. Not to mention how uncoordinated and clumsy I am by myself. If the iPad were less expensive like my Kindle Fire, I would probably go for a case that is more style than function, and a basic screen protector sheet. As it is, I have no desire to either replace the glass, or worse, buy a new iPad, so I got the super functional, heavy duty case. The iPad doesn't look as pretty in it, and the screen often looks dirty or smudged as the built-in screen protector doesn't keep it as clean looking as the stick on sheets, but it definitely does it's job.

While I like the hinge covers for the back camera and the speakers, they aren't very little kid friendly. It's easy for the kids to pull them out, and putting them back requires taking the iPad out of the case, replacing the hinged covers, then going through the effort of putting the iPad back. After doing that once, I just leave them off now. I wish there was no way for them to come off, but it isn't a deal breaker for me.

text_fidelity_a:
Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology This is a cameras that is perfect for some but not something that everyone will find useful. The ideal user is someone who wants a simple to use digital camera that has the ability to instantly print the photo without dealing with a PC or conventional printer. This does a pretty good job of accomplishing that goal. But, if you’re looking for a more advanced point and shoot with lots of image features, this may not be your best option.

The camera itself feels very solid, but lacks a key digital camera feature: a view screen. At first glance may seem to be a major omission. But, this camera is designed to be a high-tech replacement for the old-style Polaroid instant cameras by instantly (well, relatively instantly) printing the photo on Zink paper. Note that the paper needs to be purchased separately, and is pretty much an essential component for using the camera. While you can store photos on an SD card, the camera is really designed to be used with the Zink paper.

Usage is very straightforward – it’s about as point and shoot as you can get. That’s great for those who don’t want to fiddle with any settings, but it does put some constraints on image quality. I’ve had about 20% of my photos so far turn out less than ideal due to improper focus, poor white balance, poor resolution and/or incorrect color registration. That’s my major complaint with this camera – the paper is costly, and when you have to toss (or at least not really like) one in five photos, the cost can add up.

The images are small – the paper is only 2 by 3 inches. On the plus side it has a peel and stick backing, so you can use the photos as “post-its” very easily. Again, this is keeping with the intent of the camera, so I won’t downgrade the rating due to the small photo size.

Other negatives for me is that the battery is not user-replaceable. I’ve had too many electronic products with built-in batteries that had to be trashed since the internal battery no longer held a charge. I’m also not fond of the lens cap. It’s very easy to take off (it’s held in place by magnets) but there’s no attachment to the camera, so it’s very easy to misplace.

But this does score well with regard to ease of use and fun. As a test of ease of use I handed this to my Mom who is technically challenged, to say the least. She had no problems snapping photos and loved having the image print right there. She’s never liked using a digital camera in the past due to difficulty using it and dealing with image files. This was right up her ally.

While I’ll drop the rating to 4 stars due to the image quality issues that can crop up, overall this is a unique camera. It’s not right for everyone, but if you’re looking to revisit the days of the Polaroid instant camera while staying in the digital world, this is well worth considering.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology

text_fidelity_a:
FYHXele Computer Monitor, Gaming Monitor 24 Inch 75Hz, IPS FHD 1080P, 2xHDMI, USB Type-C, Built-in Speakers, Adaptive Sync, VESA for Office Home, Black I’ve been using the FYHXele 24 Inch Monitor (75Hz version) for the last month, and it has totally spoiled me for playing games on my Switch! The monitor has built-in speakers, so I can hear a game’s music while playing. It’s a small but nice feature; I can easily switch the input from my laptop to my Switch and not have to rearrange my whole desk to play games.

The picture is bright and vibrant. I’ve been playing Hades for the last month and it looks SO good on this screen. Bright and crisp, even if I play during the day. I also use the monitor as a second display for work, it’s good for that too, either as a streaming display or for text and spreadsheets.

I use it with my MacBook Pro, the monitor has 2 HDMI inputs and 1 USB-C. The USB-C port doesn’t support passthrough charging.

A VESA plate is included, which was a nice plus. I do use a monitor arm because I don’t like the stand this monitor comes with. The angle and height are not adjustable at all, and I didn’t like the default angle. The base is 9 inches by 7 inches, so it has a large footprint. I also don’t love the “FYHXele” printed in white at the bottom of the screen.

The power cable is relatively short, only 50 inches. It’s an AC adapter, not a power brick. The box also includes an HDMI cable -- another nice plus -- but unfortunately my cable had a cut in the coating, so I could see the copper wire.

Overall, I think this is a decent budget monitor. I never want to play my Switch in handheld mode anymore, the picture quality has spoiled me that much. The dual HDMI inputs make it easy to switch between work and fun; I’ve also used this as a Discord display, rotated 90° on a VESA arm.
text_fidelity_b: FYHXele Computer Monitor, Gaming Monitor 24 Inch 75Hz, IPS FHD 1080P, 2xHDMI, USB Type-C, Built-in Speakers, Adaptive Sync, VESA for Office Home, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) I received a Kindle as a gift, and it has taken over my reading life. I'm sad when a book is only available in print and delighted when there is a Kindle version. It's not AS comfortable as a print book, it's MORE comfortable than a print book. The font is amazing. It's easy to use, and for people who knit, it sits nicely in a bookstand on or a reader's pillow to read while knitting.

I have the Sony eReader. I used to own the rocket. I see the Kindle as the real future of ebooks, and I really want ebooks to succeed for a few reasons.

One is storage. If you are a bibliophile, you probably have a book army ready to take over your home. We avid readers are forced to cull our libraries to make room for new books. No more. I would suggest opening a free account with a service like Goodreads to categorize books, since with the Kindle you can't set up a "history" section and a "fantasy" section, but that's so minor. I never could keep those organized in my print library as well, and many books fall into multiple categories anyway. Do I need to mention that ebooks don't yellow and decay over time?

Two is portability. If you are the type to carry many books at once (I am--some for study and some for pleasure reading along with a newspaper) then this is the easiest way to do it.

Three is the glorious possibility that books will never go "out of print" again, because there is no "print" overhead, just a little meg sitting in a several terrabyte raid array somewhere. Books will always be a minute away.

Four is the idea that books will be instantly large print and still small, and easy to tote around. My eyes are still quite good, but I'd love to think, when age degrades them someday, I'll still be able to read the latest releases easily.

Five is the instant availability of hot books. When Brisingr came out, it was sitting on my Kindle that morning. Compare that to the sometimes day-long wait we went through for the Harry Potter books (and books that size are yet another reason ebooks rock). I love having the New York Times delivered, but can't stand it when the delivery boy loses the key and rings my bell at 4 in the morning. This is the best of both worlds.

Six is the ease of reading large online documents, such as those from Gutenberg or a friend's novel (and don't we all have someone who sends us large files to read from time to time?)

Seven is the price of the books. Everything is cheaper on the Kindle and some books are frighteningly inexpensive. I bought the Talmud for 99 cents. A collection of the first five books in the John Carter on Mars series for 99 cents. And the entire collection of the Wizard of Oz books for, you guessed it, 99 cents.

Other e-readers hit close to the mark; the Kindle got it right. I only want two things. I want color and I want Amazon to hit that goal of having every book (including comics and manga please) available for the Kindle. Overall, the day of the ebook truly arrived with the Kindle and I couldn't be happier.
text_fidelity_b: Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th)

Epson ProSense 347 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and Ultra Long Battery Life - Black I've been testing this Epson ProSense watch for the past week. I also have a 2-year-old Garmin Vivoactive HR watch that has most of the same features, but costs half as much. To the compare the two, I've been wearing one watch on each wrist and going on runs and bike rides to see how their readings compare. Both watches have daily step counters that give similar results (today, Garmin says 12044 steps while Epson says 12790 steps). 5% difference is close enough for me.

When I use the GPS exercise mode, the results start showing big differences. On today's run, Garmin recorded 4.02 miles while Epson says 3.9 miles. That's a 3% difference which is close enough for me. Garmin says 529 calories and Epson says 955 calories. Garmin says 535 feet of elevation gain and Epson says 1142 feet. I know Garmin has a barometric altimeter, while Epson is using GPS elevation, which is notoriously inaccurate. Does Epson's terrible elevation data cause a wildly inaccurate calorie count? I could not find any information on Epson's calorie calculation in their documentation, so I really cannot trust it.

Both devices give me heart rate readings with graphs by time or broken out by training zones. The numbers look close enough for my purposes. Both devices also give me maps of my route, which is is nice to have for reviewing later, especially if it is a new route to me.

The Epson is a much larger device (both width and thickness), as shown in the photo. While the Garmin is not especially attractive, at least it is relatively unobtrusive. Epson is big enough to feel clunky on my wrist, especially if I am wearing it all day (to take advantage of the step counter).

Both devices have a smartphone app that syncs your data and also sends notifications to the watch. I'm using this watch with a Google Pixel Android phone. The Garmin app by default uploads your data to the Garmin website. With Epson, you have to upload to a 3rd party website like Strava, which may not be compatible with all the data that your device is collecting.

Notifications work much better with Garmin than Epson. For incoming phone calls, both Garmin and Epson will display the caller ID or contact name so I don't have to pull out my phone to see who is calling. For incoming emails, Garmin displays the sender name and subject line, while Epson just says "you have mail". For text messages, Garmin shows the contact name and message. Epson shows no notification for text messages.

The only advantage (for my use case) that I can find with this Epson watch is the much longer battery life. Garmin claims 1 week of battery life with the GPS off or 13 hours with the GPS on. Epson claims 46 hours of battery life with the GPS on, which I suppose is great for some ultra endurance sports. For me, I never exercise more than 8 hours in a day.
text_fidelity_b: Epson ProSense 347 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and Ultra Long Battery Life - Black

SUDOKEJI 1000W Pure Sine Wave Inverter Power Inverter Peak Power 2000W 12V DC to 110V 120V AC with LED Display 3 AC Outlets & USB Port for RV Truck Boat This worked just fine for powering a few small items. When choosing what you are going to run on this add up the total wattage of all devices, then add at least 50% more to account for peaks or spikes in the power draw. For example if your coffee maker draws 500 watts, your laptop 300 watts, and your toaster 200 watts (total, 1000 watts) you should account for the extra 50% (1000watts + 500 watts (the 50%)=1500watts). In this example, a minimum 1500 watt inverter should be used.

If the item is motor driven, it requires additional start-up (surge) wattage (typically 2-3 times the continuous wattage required) to start the device. For example, a miter saw that runs at 700 watts might require 1400 watts to start up. If your inverter only supplies 1000 watts, you will not be able to start it up. In this case, you would want to select an inverter rated at least 1400 surge watts to handle start-up needs.

I understand how wattage works and for someone who doesn't, any inverter could fail if overloaded with more power than it can handle. An overload feature that automatically shuts the device off would be helpful for anyone who is unsure. This has an overload feature, but if you blow a fuse, you'll have to replace it. Do your research and know how this works, and it'll work fine.
text_fidelity_b: SUDOKEJI 1000W Pure Sine Wave Inverter Power Inverter Peak Power 2000W 12V DC to 110V 120V AC with LED Display 3 AC Outlets & USB Port for RV Truck Boat

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm FinePix J40 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Includes 2 GB SD Memory Card) The camera is $[..]for gosh sakes! It's an amazing little piece of technology. The 3X optics and 12.2MP CMOS camera are well matched in the optical train to provide a great image for casual photos adequate for most users. It's the simplest start-up I've ever seen. The viewer LCD provides a maximum size to the package. `The manual' is 7 steps of which 4 include inserting memory, battery, charging battery and turning it on. It's `point and shoot' in the extreme.

I work in the domain of optics & imaging design. My wife has a 5 year old Fuji camera of this same genre that I've gone to some lengths to compare with Nikon and Canon in this low cost market. Without getting technical ... for the old Fuji, there are no user discernable image quality differences. The Fuji optics were superior (i.e. best objective lens light capture and transfer). Take your pick between the 3 on the backend image processing system/PC interface.

My wife has carried the 5 year old Fuji in her purse every day ... that's a technically demanding reliability challenge. Fuji can be relied on to deliver the best value for money in an image capture platform if you're designing a million dollar platform or this $69 platform. You're not paying the premium for the huge advertisement budget of Nikon and Canon when you buy Fuji. I think you just get a better camera.

I can't speak to this unit's reliability for now. A 3x optical train with autofocus, f-stop, etc mechanisms and micro motors are robust to a point. They will all fail, even the highest dollar product, if exposed to the wrong environment (g-shock, sand, salt spray, thermal shock, etc).

One reviewer mentioned software loading problems. I had absolutely no problems on a Windows 7, 64bit OS.

You can't go wrong with this device. It's an excellent camera for you or the kids or the g-kids for Xmas.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix J40 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Includes 2 GB SD Memory Card)

I will start with the app that the instructions tell you that you need to download. It states that it is for updates, but all I saw is that it is used for is linking multiple speakers together.

I knew that I wanted something that was water proof for both of those settings so I was happy to give this one a try. As I mentioned before, this sucker is HEAVY so while it may be water proof, if you were to drop in the river at any point it would go straight to the bottom never to be seen again, so it wouldn't really matter how water proof it is. For the pool and sitting stationary, it would be perfect.

One use that I can see us using this speaker would be for travel baseball games. It is loud enough that you would be able to hear it from a distance.

As I said earlier... some will love this speaker and think that it is absolutely worth it. Others will not. This speaker will strictly come down to personal opinion. For instance, other than the weight, I love this speaker. My spouse thinks that his $50 is much better.

text_fidelity_a:
Manfrotto 3-Way Pan/Tilt Head with RC2 Quick Release Plate (MH804-3WUS) I am writing one review for my entire purchase - it just makes sense that you know about the entire setup.

I bought the Manfrotto 808RC4 along with their 190XPROB Pro Tripod and the Manfrotto MB MSTRAP-1 Tripod Carrying Strap. All at Amazon. Here's why:

This head gives you unlimited control in all directions. The large knurled handles allow you to grip and adjust the tension on the pivot points to any degree you want. I use it to pan video, I use it to do off center composure and metering. I love how rock steady this thing is when I am shooting my 60and 120 second exposures with my 300MM lens. Rock steady. And the rotation is greased smooth, nary a glitch.

With a bubble level and two straight levels you always know where you are. And gradients to indicate -30 to +90 tilt for replication. Great for panning video or shooting stills for a panorama. There are two "softening springs" to slow the movement of the tilts as you reach either end. You can disengage them if you wish.

I have friends that went with the ball heads. And regret it. They are fast, but not accurate, especially with a long lens. With this head you can adjust the tension and just ease the camera around without having to adjust it again.

Now hear me on this. I see other reviewers not so happy with the way the shoe is a little tricky. Let me say that by practicing with the shoe mounted to your camera and paying close attention snap it onto the head three times and you know all you need to know. You may have to practice a few more times to get it in the dark but I tell you that you are going to love it. When you snap the camera onto the head it automatically engages and you have no worries. The double safety has stopped me from dropping my camera twice. Lesson learned at no cost.

As to the tripod - sturdy is the word that comes to mind. And NOT overly weighty. Together the head and tripod are 7 lbs. With the strap - which I did not buy at first - this rig is rock solid and you won't even know you are carrying it. I don't even notice the combo. I hike several hours at a time and have been know to stop in a panic on the way out and feel on my back to see if the whole thing is still there! I think a big part of the "weight" issue is how it is carried. In your hands it feels hefty. On your hips, 7 lbs feels weighty. Across your shoulder diagonally, head down? It ain't even there!

The tripod has a wonderfully steady center column assembly that comes up and tilts over to the horizontal - great for macro shots or simply needing to place the camera where you aren't. The legs are sturdy and the snap retainers have just the right tension - not too hard to snap open or closed, not so loose that you worry whether one might slide. I also like that the center column is not attached to the legs with the typical arms of lesser well made tripods. Makes for very easy folding and stowing. I love the leg angle presets - easy to use and not worried about them slipping. The rubber grips on two of the legs are a hand saver in chilly weather. Nice touch.

So, in case you haven't figured it out, I love this rig. If I were going trekking across country for days I might want a little less weight, but for day long trips, portraiture or car trips this is the ticket.
text_fidelity_b: Manfrotto 3-Way Pan/Tilt Head with RC2 Quick Release Plate (MH804-3WUS)

After dithering for a couple of weeks, I finally took the plunge and ordered the kindle the day before surgery. I had a small satchel (guy purse) to carry wallet, kindle and phone with me when in therapy. My arms were too weak to hold the book I had with me. Friends brought my kindle to me the 3rd day. I then read about 5 to 6 hours or more a day and night. Charging was fast and I had no issues with battery life. I charged once a day. If needed I could read while kindle was charging. I bought the 3g and wi-fi addition. Downloaded on both as hospital wi-fi quit sometimes at night. Holding a book to read had become a chore for me some years ago. Sitting at a table reading was uncomfortable, therefore I have neglected to my reading. I have downloaded Edgar A. Poe's works. I especially enjoy his comic and scientific pieces. text_fidelity_a:
Nitecore SC2 Superb Charger 3A Quick Charge Bundle with EASTSHINE EB182 Battery Organizer Overall, this is a solid charger. The build quality is top-notch, it’s sized so that you don’t have to struggle to put in/take out 26650s, and the 3A charge rate is a treat. However, it has a design issue that, while not a major roadblock, can be quite irritating.

Let’s start with the good news. This is one solidly-built charger. Compared with other chargers in its general price class from Efest and Xtar, this has a lot more heft to it. The sliders are perfect – not too loose; not too tight – and move smoothly without any crunchiness or squeaking. Best of all, it can hold two 26650s without any difficulty getting them in or out of the slots. That’s a great feature since I’ve been using a lot more 26650 mods recently, and getting those fat batteries in or out of some of my Xtar chargers is a major pain.

Other ease of use features include non-slip feet on the base that keep it firmly planted. The included power cord does not have a wall wart on the end – just a regular plug – which is a welcome change. All in all I have absolutely zero complaints about the fit and finish.

Performance is also solid. Each slot is independent, and can be set to charge at up to 3A. However, only one channel can be set at 3A since the total cannot exceed 5A. But even one 3A channel is a great feature if you use large capacity 26650s that can support a 3A input. It cuts the recharge time to the bone. It also has a USB output for charging (2.1A). However, you must leave slot 2 empty if you want the USB charging to take priority. Otherwise, it will charge the cell in slot 2 first, then charge via USB.

The charger has all the customary protection features that you would expect from a good quality charger such as overtime protection, reverse polarity protection, and auto shut off if it runs more than 10 hours. It also has a recovery mode for deeply discharged Li-ion cells. I never use that (if I accidently deeply discharge a cell I no longer use it) but it has the feature should it be of value for your needs. Heat output when running was very low.

The current for each slot can be set to 0.5A, 1A, 2A or 3A. You can also set the cutoff voltage to 1.2v, 3.7v, 4.2v or 4.3v. I use this nearly only with Li-ion cells, so the 4.2v cutoff is what I use for most of my charging. However, it’s nice to have the 3.7v setting for when I want to charge cells for long-term storage.

If you do nothing, the charger will set itself to a 2A current for cells that are greater than 1200mAh, and 0.5A for cells less than 1200mAh. You can override the settings for both current and cutoff independently for each channel.

And that’s where the biggest irritation occurs. The charger has a double row of LED lights that signify current and cutoff levels (plus blink to show operation, and stop blinking when charging is done). Simple and unobtrusive. However, there are no notations on the screen to show what charge rate/cutoff corresponds to each LED. Instead, those numbers are listed on a piece of clear plastic that is stuck on top of the display. It peels off easily and looks like a temporary cover to protect the screen.

In addition to looking poor, the lack of durability of the cover with the numbers listed means it won’t survive for long. Now, there are only four positions for the LEDs so it’s not a huge puzzler to decipher the settings if you use the charger regularly. However, I have several chargers and can go a couple of weeks between using one in particular. It can be hard to remember which LED position means what. And I shouldn’t have to do that – numbers should be imprinted right on the screen and not on a flimsy piece of plastic.

I also don’t care for the fact that the button labels (one for current, one for cutoff) are embossed into the plastic. The black-on-black makes it very hard to see which button is which.

But those issues aside, this is a solid charger that offers up to 3A charging. The build quality and operation are both excellent, and it’s perfectly sized to hold two 26650 cells without a bit of struggle to get them in or out of the slots. The poorly designed screen and button labels drops my score to 4.5 stars, but I’ll round up since everything else is well executed.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Nitecore SC2 Superb Charger 3A Quick Charge Bundle with EASTSHINE EB182 Battery Organizer

Noctua NA-FC1, 4-Pin PWM Fan Controller (Black) This is the only PWM controller I could find that works. It works very well. You can outright control a PWM fan straight from a power supply or by modifying an existing PWM fan signal from the motherboard. This is designed to be able to drive multiple fans daisy-chained together by having the power option be applied after the signal is modified.

I have tried to find PWM fan controllers, but most controllers that I came across are voltage based which does not work well for granular low speed control. This works well for that. The anti-stall feature did not work for me, but it is not a concern for me.

text_fidelity_a:
Anker Ergonomic Optical USB Wired Vertical Mouse 1000/1600 DPI, 5 Buttons CE100 The mouse functions fine and I do like the form of it. There is one critical problem though. The form forces the forward and back buttons to be on the opposite side of left and right click so while your thumb is on the forward or back, you have no choice but to squeeze the right or left click to engage the forward/back button. Obviously, this causes inadvertent clicks with the mouse which is a problem. It happens mainly on the forward button as this is where the left and right click start to engage, too (more forward on the mouse itself).

I have not decided if I will keep it or not as I rely heavily on the use of these buttons. If I can find a way to grip it so this does not occur, it will be fine. In the meantime, I'll be using it look for a mouse that is designed better.

UPDATE 2-23-16: Like many others who have posted less than favorable reviews, Anker customer support has reached out to me directly, twice, offering a full refund, which I declined. In my opinion, the mouse works well for it's price, but I stand by the issue noted above. I have gotten used to is and can grip the mouse slightly differently when using the forward button. For this reason and for the outstanding customer service, I have bumped the review to 3 stars and wouldn't hesitate to recommend trying it out given the extremely low risk.
text_fidelity_b: Anker Ergonomic Optical USB Wired Vertical Mouse 1000/1600 DPI, 5 Buttons CE100

SABRENT USB 2.0 to DB25 IEEE 1284 Parallel Printer Cable Adapter [HEXNUT Connectors] (CB-1284) Although every new printer has a USB port, I have a few older, but still perfectly functioning printers that only have parallel inputs. I've been using those printers with PCs that have a parallel output port but, as those PCs get retired, it's getting harder to find a way to hook up the old printers. This solves that problem very well.

It's a simple cable. One end is a USB plug; the other is a DB25 female parallel port. IMPORTANT: you want to check your printer to make sure it can accept a DB25 female plug. Many printers only have a 36-pin Centronics input. If so, you need to get this one: [[ASIN:B00IDU0T1Y Sabrent USB to Parallel IEEE 1284 Printer Cable Adapter (CB-CN36)]]

The cable itself is decent. Thin, but the jacket feels more than sturdy enough for the job at hand. It's only 6 foot long which is OK for my needs but just barely. A longer version (10 or 12 foot) would be nice.

Works fine, and no complaints.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: SABRENT USB 2.0 to DB25 IEEE 1284 Parallel Printer Cable Adapter [HEXNUT Connectors] (CB-1284)

If I wanted anything fancier, I'd get a tablet, but when I got this I wanted all of the feelings of a book without the bulkiness when I travel. I'll be sad when it goes, but so far, so good. The battery lasts for ages, I can go months without turning it on, and it'll start right up, and it's durable. The only drawback is there are no page numbers, only long and lengthy location numbers so if you lose your page by keeping it turned on and tossing it in a  bag, or a kid grabs it and taps it, you're SOL.

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Harmony 700 Rechargeable Remote with Color Screen (Black) [Discontinued by Manufacturer] Solid remote with major flaws. Yes, the battery does last a long time...no issue there. But there is no battery life indicator on the screen and you don't get any warning when running low. So unless you plug it in regularly (which defeats the purpose of long battery life) you go from working perfectly to dead with no warning. While plugged in a battery graphic with a bolt tells you it's charging, but doesn't tell you the % charged or when it is done. When you unplug it the battery graphic doesn't go away, and it doesn't return to normal operation. You can push all the buttons you want, the battery graphic stays on the screen and it doesn't work. The only way to get it working is to take out the batteries and put them back in. And after you do that, you have to go through the tutorial before you can start using it again (thankfully, it does retain the device programming). What a hassle.

And when is Harmony going to get rid of the remote assistant? Like previous models, it constantly asks you if you want to hide the assistant, and it won't operate until you answer. Does the assistant even do anything the help button doesn't? If Harmony is so in love with this outdated 1990s feature, just put an assistant button on the remote and keep the damn thing hidden unless WE decide to turn it on. And the ability to skip the tutorial would be nice too. Nobody wants to be constantly answering to their remote.

Harmony is very good at making initial programming of the remote easy, but seem to give up on the interface after that. Once I'm done programming it, I don't want to mess with it any more, and I CERTAINLY don't want it to interrupt operation. Do what I ask you to do, otherwise sit there and look pretty.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Harmony 700 Rechargeable Remote with Color Screen (Black) [Discontinued by Manufacturer]

text_fidelity_a:
(Discontinued) HP ENVY 32-Inch Screen LED-Lit Monitor Quad-HD There's a lot to like about this monitor, but also some clear drawbacks. Let's start with the good news.

In typical HP fashion it comes very well packaged to survive pretty much any measure of rough handling in transit. There's a "quick start" guide that is taped to the front of the monitor that walks you through the setup (which is very straightforward). There's also an excellent user guide in PDF on the included disk.

The overall design is very attractive. It's very slim, lightweight and easy to position. I'm using it with the included table stand since my wall-mount options can't handle a monitor this large (it does come with a metal plate with VESA-compatible holes should you want to use it with a mount).

I used this on both a PC and as a video monitor hooked up through my AV receiver. For both situations I used the HDMI interface.

The sound quality is very good compared with the typical built-in speaker. It lacks bass "punch" but is quite acceptable.

Now for the so-so news: picture quality. It's good, but not "wow" good. Picture quality was somewhat drab looking, lacking crispness and contrast despite spending a lot of time tweaking the video quality with the many options available. It becomes worse when viewed off center (although it does have a decent viewing angle).

It comes with a remote which could be very handy for switching inputs, tweaking the picture, adjusting the sound, etc. I say it "could be" since the remote it comes with is horrible. It's small, which is good, but all the buttons are flush mount and have black on black lettering. It is very, very hard to see which button is which even in bright light. Forget about finding the right button in dim light. Truly horrible design work.

While there are pluses, and it is hitting an attractive price point, I can't see this being worthy of anything more than a little above average (3.5 star) rating. It's a decent, but not exceptional monitor (with a total design failure of a remote). Worth considering if you are looking for a large monitor without breaking the bank, and have moderate expectations as to video quality.
text_fidelity_b: (Discontinued) HP ENVY 32-Inch Screen LED-Lit Monitor Quad-HD

Cons: Horrible sound output!

Sorry, but I'm not 100% convinced these aren't knock-offs. I bought these to replace a different pair of stock Samsung earbuds for my Note 4 after my dog decided they looked like a good snack.

After actually using through a morning commute, I'm confident with the conclusion that these are either knock-offs or refurbished. They have horrible sound output!

I'm not am audiophile and I don't expect stock earbuds to "wow" me with their amazing range. But with these there's NO bass whatsoever. The range seems to be limited to the higher notes. Everything sounds hollow too. I have to turn the volume up way past the recommended volume to hear much of anything.

I guess another was of putting it is that these are a GREAT pair of $7.00 earbuds. They don't seem like a decent replacement for the stock Samsung earbuds that came with my Note 4.

Are these really Samsung earbuds?

text_fidelity_a:
Razer Opus Active Noise Cancelling ANC Wireless Headphones: THX Audio Tuning - 25 Hr Battery - Bluetooth 4.2 & 3.5mm Jack Compatible - Auto Play/Auto Pause - Carrying Case Included - Midnight Blue At first glance, the Razer Opus ANC Wireless Headphones don’t look like a Razer product. Where’s the green? Where’s the RGB? Even the branding is subdued.

These headphones are a grown-up Razer product, probably meant to be headphones you can take anywhere and not stick out as a gamer.

The Midnight Blue color is a nice change from black. I have a few pairs of wireless headphones and every single pair is black, so I appreciate having a little variety. Midnight Blue is a very deep blue -- so deep it’s almost black.

I’ve been trying the Opus headphones out for a few weeks and they have become the headphones I use every day. Before, I was using the Sony XB900N.

My favorite thing about the Opus headphones is how comfortable they are. The headband and ear cups have cushy padding. The headphones don’t squeeze my head too tight and don’t weigh a lot. I can wear these for 5+ hours at a time and not get a headache.

Sound quality is decent. I mostly use the Opus for listening to music and TV/movies. Compared to Razer’s gaming headsets, this isn’t one I’d pick for serious gaming. There is a tiny bit of lag and the low, deep sounds aren’t as punchy as with say, a Razer Kraken headset.

Razer’s claim of up to 25 hours of battery life seems pretty accurate. I didn’t keep a log every time I used the headphones, but I was able to use them for 4-5 hours a day for a good week before needing to charge. Unfortunately there is no battery indicator on the headphones to know when the battery is running low.

I don’t love the Razer Opus app needed to tweak a few of the settings. I have an older Android phone running Nougat, the app is incompatible with my phone. So I had to borrow my mom’s iPhone to install the app. By default, the headphones shut off after 5 minutes and I could only change this setting in the app. The app also allows you to switch between a few audio presets (but you can’t create your own) and check battery life.

If I take the headphones off my head, they automatically pause whatever I’m watching or listening to. I like this; my mom often talks to me when I’m wearing headphones, so it’s a lot quicker to just take them off and now I don’t have to manually pause. This is a setting that can be changed in the app.

The Active Noise Cancelling is what I expect for a pair of headphones in this price range. It’s decent. Not great, not horrible, but good enough to mute most background noise. But I don’t like that there’s not a light or indicator on the headphones to tell when I have ANC turned on.

The Opus doesn’t support Bluetooth multipoint.

The headphones charge via USB-C. The included case stores the headphones, charging cable, USB-C to USB A adapter, 3.5 mm audio cable, and airline adapter. The case actually has an outline on the bottom to tell you how to fit the headphones inside.
text_fidelity_b: Razer Opus Active Noise Cancelling ANC Wireless Headphones: THX Audio Tuning - 25 Hr Battery - Bluetooth 4.2 & 3.5mm Jack Compatible - Auto Play/Auto Pause - Carrying Case Included - Midnight Blue

Made in Taiwan is a positive thing. Be aware that illegitimate cards do exist. Illegitimate in this case meaning falsified capacity. I've had one that actually reads as its rated capacity, but only "remembers" the last 20 MB or so.

Comes packaged like a normal card, in a small blister pack with a full size SD adapter. No reusable plastic case inside the blister pack, but most of us already have some of those (and don't really need them anyway).

VideoSecu Low Profile TV Wall Mount Bracket for Most 32" - 75" LCD LED UHD Plasma HDTV, Compatible with Sony Bravia Samsung LG Haier Vizio Sharp AQUOS Westinghouse Pioneer ProScan Toshiba 1NN The bracket is incredible! I used it on a Samsung Plasma 60 inch ,(600x400-Vesa) PN60F5500. At first I was a little wary. The plasma is 2013 model ,weighs by itself about 60 pounds.Its solid, and the weight of my TV held it down without using security brackets. You need at least an 18 inch long screw driver because you cannot reach behind it once installed. A few turns and you're set. I found it easier to unscrew , first tighten , then go in the opposite direction so it locks the screwdriver in the center making it easier to remove. I left it untighten, since it held in place without them.

Im not a professional installer (like drilling holes and finding a stud in the wall) but was able to use my old screws from the wall to install this mount from my older plasma.. I did however have to drill 2 more at the bottom because of the Vesa difference. Beyond that, everything else was simple.Its solid once installed, very easy, and simple to understand.

CON: Personal pet peeve. The only con is on 60 inch TVs you cannot reach behind easily to use the security brackets.You have to use an 18 inch long screw driver or similar size to tighten them. (booklet does not say this . Only says use a screwdriver)They are not needed because the weight of the TV holds in in place. In my opinion, I like to do everything by the instructions. Not tighten the security brackets made me feel like I skipped a step. I will say its stays in place, and does not move, jiggle etc. Lifting the bottom of a 60 inch is not easy, so there is no worry about it being easily done, even by a kid since the hooks are on the top. Other reviewers have said security brackets are not needed to hold it in place. I just left them barely connected so I could have the option to screw on later.

PS: If you own a 60 inch and im guessing 65 (max size), it will not look like the picture after adding the back portions on the TV. At first I was under the impression it would not work, but adjusted the height on the TV brackets and it fit barely, but did fit.It does work on a (600x400) vesa mount TV.
text_fidelity_b: VideoSecu Low Profile TV Wall Mount Bracket for Most 32" - 75" LCD LED UHD Plasma HDTV, Compatible with Sony Bravia Samsung LG Haier Vizio Sharp AQUOS Westinghouse Pioneer ProScan Toshiba 1NN

I started looking for something around that size and stumbled on this one for not too much more than a smaller one. So, I figured I'd give it a try, and if I liked it, I'd put the 32 inch tv from my living room in the bedroom.

Set up was very easy. I put it together using the stand. I had enough screws. They all fit. You have to screw them all the way in straight, or the tv kind of wobbles on the stand, but once I did that, the thing is very stable.

It has one component input, one composite, one antenna, one VGA, and three hdmi, and I'm using all of them. Very very easy. the whole thing, including moving the other tv, took half an hour, with the only slight pain being that my late 2010 Mac Mini won't under scan at 1080p, so I had to go to 720p, on the hdmi connection. I don't even know what any of that means, except that this is what I had to do in order to be able to see my menu bar.

Picture is really nice for the price, even my little intel atom its box over the VGA looks good. What impressed me most is the sound. I only use the tv's speakers for the Wii U, and they are surprisingly clear. I'm still figuring out some of the settings, but up and running in half an hour and enjoying the results is pretty amazing - especially for the price.

text_fidelity_a:
ZUGU CASE - 2019 iPad Air 10.5/2017 iPad Pro 10.5 inch Case Prodigy X - Very Protective But Thin + Convenient Magnetic Stand + Sleep/Wake Cover (Purple) Update: A good pencil sleeve to use with this case after stretching it out a bit with a crayola dry erase marker is the Hydream Silicone Case for Apple Pencil Holder Sleeve Skin Pocket Cover Accessories for iPad Pro 9.7/10.5/12.9, Cute Soft Grip Pouch with Charging Cap Holder and 2 Protective Nib Covers.

TL:DR - a fantastic case and looks amazing with a screen protector on the device. Does not interfere with screen protectors at all. Great utility and angle options. Looks good on the fridge too. If you don't mind the case feeling a bit awkward to hold when looking at things in portrait and the fact that your Pencil Sleeve options are limited due to the super tight elastic (I used a crayola dry eraser to stretch mine and now the fit perfect) this is the case for you.

Pros:
8 Adjustment points
The packaging and info included on the company
The quality
The looks (at least in black for me)
The pencil sleeve built in
The wake/sleep utility
Solid positions minus the last one if you're really pretty on it. Like heavy handed drawing hard.

Cons:
The tablet is hard to hold in portrait especially if the pencil is in the case
I know the 2018 Pro model had yet to be released when this case was made, but I wish the placement of the Pencil sleeve was in a better location or allowed enough space for a wider variety of pencil sleeves. It makes me worry that it sticks out a little from the case. Kinda wish it was on the top or had a similar elastic sleeve loop on the top where an Apple Pencil 2 would sit magnetically. More or a nitpick though.
The tightness of the sleeve out of the box! This was very annoying, but another nitpick since I can always stretch it out.
A little awkward to use the rear-facing camera since when holding with the front panel touching the back of the case it covers the camera completely. Even when in landscape you have to tilt it high enough to free your view.

Quality of Life Cons: (basically super nitpicks. Feel free to ignore. The case is great!)
Would have been nice if they added another small sleeve near the rear pencil sleeve for the small charging Pencil dongle. It looks like there is enough room in the back.
Like the little indents where the power and volume buttons are located I'd have liked to see a little notch above the charging port center of the charging port. Why? Because I often find myself inserting the connector low of the actual charging port and a little notch where the middle would generally be would have been a nice touch or at least some more material to alleviate confusion on the port's location. If you look at the charging port with the case on you'll see what I mean, there is a little lip which can make it confusing on what I'm inserting the plug into (done this a lot lately, but getting better at it).
A somewhat more rigid hinge on the panel that covers the screen. Why? It can get really floppy when holding it in portrait mode and a slightly more rigid hinge kind of like the surface pro keyboard cover would have been nice. The panel itself is solid but the material connecting it to the case can be a little floppy.
text_fidelity_b: ZUGU CASE - 2019 iPad Air 10.5/2017 iPad Pro 10.5 inch Case Prodigy X - Very Protective But Thin + Convenient Magnetic Stand + Sleep/Wake Cover (Purple)

Digital Photo Frame 15-inch WiFi Digital Picture Frame - FULLJA Smart Digital Photo Frames 32GB Storage, Easy to Setup and Share Photos and Videos via App or Email, Gifts for Family The Fullja 10 inch WiFi Digital Picture Frame replaces >5-year-old LCD frame. Wow. Excellent upgrade in both hardware and software.

The total frame size is 10" x 7" in practical terms. The IPS (in-plane switching) touch-screen LCD at 1280x800 resolution (189 PPI) is HD, one LCD grade less than FHD. I can't discriminate between HD and FHD resolution from a picture frame's typical viewing distance. The LCD viewing angle is excellent, consistent with the IPS fabrication. This is important, perhaps THE most important criteria for an LCD picture frame. The LCD's backlighting is motion-activated and quite good. Backlighting consumes most of the battery current. Motion detection will extend battery life.

Clock, calendar, and weather update options expand the utility beyond a picture frame. Image connectivity and control include the range from TF portable memory to WiFi. Very cool.

Better than expected. Excellent value for money. One wonders how it can be made at the price.

It's a good way of keeping your machine safe from malware attacks. No need to purchase and renew antiviral software. The screen is clear and bright, and the keyboard works really nicely. The sound from these is much better than the sound on my much more expensive laptop. Overall, the size and functionality of the Chromebook is much better than my new Windows 8.1 laptop.

My kids were able to get started immediately with minimal help from me to download some apps they like, get their e-mails set up and started using these Chromebooks immediately. I personally am not nuts about having only Google Chrome as my internet browser, thus I don't own my own Chromebook, but for my kids purposes (mainly games and schoolwork) the Chromebooks work out great. I really like how easy and smoothly they work. They are faster than my laptop and I do find that appealing, but I like being able to use a DVD drive and to be able to download what software I might want from the internet.

Printing is possible from the cloud and set up to do that is not difficult. Everything is easy........almost too easy. You can't store any data on the computer itself, only in the cloud. But, I'm not worried about any personal information being accessed by nefarious types because there's really nothing to access.

We've had these Chromebooks since Christmas and they are still working fine with no problems whatsoever.

UPDATE: 2.28.15 - My daughter brought it to my attention that these chromebooks do not have a "delete" key. Interesting.

Bluetooth Headphones Wireless Earbuds Sports Over-Ear Bluetooth 5.3 Ear Buds with Earhooks 120H Playtime Wireless Headphones for Workout Waterproof Audifonos Bluetooth inalambricos LED Power Display I find that the best price to performance is in the $30 range for Bluetooth headphones, and they keep getting better and better. I have several pairs that I use for the gym, general listening to music, watching movies, and playing poker. I like to have other charged ones ready to go if a pair gets low.

These were rated very well, so I decided to give them a shot. They are super comfortable and they stay in place at the gym. I am not an audiophile, but these are well balanced and have better sound quality than my other pairs.

The greatest thing about these is the battery life- I used them for about 11 hours, and there was still 50% battery life left. With all my other pairs the battery life is a real problem, and it does not improve as they age. The charging case is also nice and there is a display for remaining battery life of the case. Remaining battery life of the headphones is displayed on the mobile device.

The BT connection is also super reliable. I have not experienced any disconnects or interference.

There are a couple cons (no product is perfect) and I want to briefly discuss them.

1. The rubber snap-on ear buds are not universal. They have a unique oval shape where they snap on and are secured. I have a bunch of spares, but they will not fit on here. If you lose one or it breaks it is useless. It comes with 3 sizes, but most people are probably like me and can only use the one size that fits.

2. The gain is too high on these. Adjusting the volume from zero, there are not many steps until the volume is too high. This means that micro-adjustment of the volume is not possible. All my other pairs I can use at 100% volume or near this (though I would not recommend it) and there there are maybe 15 or more micro-adjustments all the way back down to zero. Also, the notifications "power on," "power off," and "connected" are too loud. It's possible that with different mobile phones they behave differently, and there may also be an adjustment for this.

In summary, I highly recommend these. They are comfortable, they stay in place, they stay connected to my device, and they sound great. Probably the biggest Pro is the battery life. I purchased these to use as a backup for my other pairs, but it turns out that these will be my main headphones.
text_fidelity_b: Bluetooth Headphones Wireless Earbuds Sports Over-Ear Bluetooth 5.3 Ear Buds with Earhooks 120H Playtime Wireless Headphones for Workout Waterproof Audifonos Bluetooth inalambricos LED Power Display

text_fidelity_a:
Canon Cameras US PowerShot SX720 HS Black My SX280 HS is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 lens errors. This is the closest replacement, AFAIK. The 40x zoom is probably not that useful, since the 280's 20x was right at the limit of stable framing, but no biggie. I just like the SX HS series with the DIGIC 6 processor. I looked at the 730, but didn't need Bluetooth & didn't like the look of the oversimplified controls. And $50 buys a couple of extra batteries.

One thing you do get for several years of technology development is a better battery/sensor. Thus far the 720 shows no sign of gobbling electricity the way the 280 does. The extra $100 also buys a better written manual. I discovered a couple of minor features both cameras have, but which you'd be hard pressed to figure out from the 280's manual.--9/2/2017
Update: The 280's video/battery life problems are fixed in the 720. Image stabilization is very good. I got acceptable results at >20x zoom with a light-weight monopod (a Slik). Close focus also appears much better.--9/4/2017
I'm still on my first battery charge!--9/17/2017
Update: I fixed the 280's lens errors with a can of air and a heavy hand blowing out the gaps in the lens. Risky, but it worked. The 720 is still my go to camera. I upped the rating to 5.
July 2019 Update--I got a killer deal on a Panasonic Lumix ZS70. Great camera ... but ... it feels a lot bigger than this one in my hand. It has more features, does more things, but the 720 is lighter, handier, and in some cases takes better still pictures. If you don't need an EVF, tilt-screen and better video, this (or its SX740HS successor) might just be the better choice. The 740 has a tilt-screen.
June 2020
One word of advice. The sensor is 20 Mpx. The lens is capable of delivering 5-8 Mpx. This is typical of these small cameras. Don't be afraid to use lower resolutions or higher compressions. You won't lose much. Still a favorite camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon Cameras US PowerShot SX720 HS Black

text_fidelity_a:
Canon EOS 5D Mark II 21.1MP Full Frame CMOS Digital SLR Camera with EF 24-105mm f/4 L IS USM Lens (OLD MODEL) I've used and throughly enjoyed a 5D for a couple of years, and have found it to be a simply outstanding full-frame camera. Like a lot of people, I was eagerly looking forward to the 5D Mark II, and pre-ordered one. After using it for a few weeks, I am pleased to report that this is an excellent update to the 5D.

If you're researching this camera, you've probably heard about the "black dot" problem (basically, some dark pixels to the right of blown highlights). Unless you're printing photos in the several feet by several feet size, you'll never see them. Sure, I'll download a firmware fix when it's available, but in the meantime, I've never encountered even the slightest problem in real-world use.

Size and controls are very comparable to the 5D - you'll feel at ease very quickly. The viewfinder is fantastic -- bigger, brighter, and a very welcome addition. There are many "under the skin" upgrades, the biggest being 21.1 megapixels. So much more flexibility in shooting, but be prepared for some huge raw files! A processor upgrade (DIGIC 4) keeps things moving along at a good clip. I can't comment on the HD video capture since I'm just dabbling with it at the moment and have essentially no experience as a videographer. But, looking forward to learning. The video capture was just icing on the cake for me - bought it for still photos.

Disappointments are very few and far between, such as the fact that the battery pack is a different design, so it can't be interchanged with the 5D. Supposedly, it has a longer life, but model interchangeability would be nice to keep the add-on costs down. I also regularly shoot with my 40D and Rebel (with the latter converted to IR), so the greater the interchangeability, the better.

In short, this is an outstanding camera, and one that will be a welcome addition to anyone's kit. If you already have a 5D and use it a lot, the Mark II is well worth the cost. The kit is a good value versus the body -- the 24-105 f/4 L IS is one of the best walk around lens available. Should you not have a need for it, you can get a good price for it on the used market.

If you're presently working with a crop sensor camera, you will be amazed at what a full frame will do for you (although, be prepared to spend some coin on some good glass -- once you get the L lens fever, you'll never want to go back!). Keep in mind that the original 5D is still available, and going at a very nice price new (and some outright steals for used bodies). The original is still a fantastic camera, and well worth considering if budget is tight.

One final point -- the RAW files are not compatable with CS3. But, the recent update to Lightroom (2.2) solves that problem. No need to update to CS4 just for that.
text_fidelity_b: Canon EOS 5D Mark II 21.1MP Full Frame CMOS Digital SLR Camera with EF 24-105mm f/4 L IS USM Lens (OLD MODEL)
